phonics.tipJa: どうしに -tion を つけると「～する こと・もの」と いう なまえの ことばに なるよ。invent（はつめいする）→ invention（はつめい）、protect（まもる）→ protection、collect（あつめる）→ collection、connect（つなぐ）→ connection。-tion は「シュン」と よわく いおう。

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, The future is something that we create together. Then the clock door under the square opened. Today, we walk down some old stone stairs. Tick, tock. Tick, tock. At the bottom, there is a very long hallway. It is full of doors. Each door has a different picture on it. Then a tall grandfather clock walks toward us! His pendulum swings from side to side, and his face is round and kind. He bows and says, Welcome to the Corridor of Time! I'm Old Tock, the keeper of the corridor. Each door opens to a different time. Say it with me. Each door opens to a different time. Great! Old Tock gives us an old paper map. It's the Time Map! There are six empty holes on it, and they are shaped like gears. Let's read the note on the back of the map. "The Time Map. This map belongs to brave travelers who want to learn about the past. Open the doors, listen to the people, and ask good questions. Find out how people lived, worked, and played long ago. When you finish each part of your journey, a golden gear will click into one of the six holes. When all six gears shine, the last door will open. Take your time, and enjoy every door. Old Tock, Keeper of the Corridor." How many holes are there on the map? Six. What happens when all six gears shine? The last door will open. Now, phonics. Today, we change a verb into a noun. Add t, i, o, n, and say shun. Invent, invention. Protect, protection. Collect, collection. Connect, connection. This corridor is a connection between now and long ago. Next time, we will open the first door and walk on a very old road!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Each door opens to a different time. Today, Old Tock opens the first door. Creak! We step onto a dusty road between green hills. There are no cars and no trains. A man with a big pack on his back walks past us. He has a walking stick and straw sandals. Old Tock says, Long ago, there were no cars. People used to walk to faraway towns. Used to（むかしは ～した） means people did something many times in the past, but they don't do it now. Say it with me. People used to walk to faraway towns. Wonderful! Haru asks, How long did it take? Old Tock says, Sometimes it took many days. Next to the road, there is an old wooden sign. Let's read it. "Welcome, travelers, to the Pine Tree Rest House. The next town is two days away on foot. Rest here, drink some tea, and dry your sandals by the fire. Long ago, travelers used to stop at rest houses like this one every night. They shared food and stories with strangers. Many of them carried only a small bag, a hat, and a walking stick. Please be careful on the mountain road. Safe travels!" How far is the next town? Two days away on foot. What did travelers share? Food and stories. Is this a fact or an opinion? Walking is the best way to see the world. That's an opinion. Kiko thinks walking is slow. Riko thinks walking is fun because you can see flowers and birds. Both are OK! Now, phonics. Change the verb into a noun with a, t, i, o, n, and say ay-shun. Explore, exploration. Imagine, imagination. Inform, information. Prepare, preparation. A long trip needed lots of preparation! Next time, we will visit an old house with no phones!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, People used to walk to faraway towns. Today, Old Tock opens a door with a small wooden handle. We are inside an old house. The floor has soft tatami mats, and there is a paper lamp in the corner. A girl is sitting at a low table. She is writing with a brush. Old Tock says, Long ago, there were no phones, so people wrote letters. Say it with me. There were no phones, so people wrote letters. Excellent! Kiko is surprised. No phones? How did people talk to faraway friends? Old Tock smiles. They wrote letters, and then they waited. It took a week for a letter to arrive. The girl shows us her letter. Let's read it. "Dear Grandma, How are you? It's getting cold here, and the leaves on our big tree are turning red. Yesterday, I helped Mother make rice cakes. My little brother ate three! I miss you very much. I used to see you every day when you lived next door. Now you live far away, so I write to you every month. Please write back soon. I will wait by the door for the mail carrier. With love, Hana." Who is the letter for? Her grandma. How often does Hana write? Every month. Is this a fact or an opinion? Letters are better than messages. It's an opinion. Letters are slow, but they feel special. Messages are fast and easy. Both have good points. Now, phonics. Change the verb into a noun with m, e, n, t, and say ment. Develop, development. Move, movement. Achieve, achievement. Improve, improvement. The telephone was a big improvement for families who lived far apart. Next time, we will visit a room full of old toys!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, There were no phones, so people wrote letters. Today, Old Tock opens a bright red door. Ding, ding! It's a toy room! There are spinning tops, cloth dolls, paper kites, and glass marbles. Everything looks old, but it's beautiful. Birimo picks up a wooden top and spins it on the floor. Old Tock says, Long ago, there were no video games. Children used to play with wooden toys. Say it with me. Children used to play with wooden toys. Super! Riko asks, Where did they get them? Old Tock says, Many children used to make their own toys. They cut wood, folded paper, and sewed cloth. There is a card on a glass case. Let's read it. "Toys from Long Ago. These toys are about one hundred years old. Most of them are made of wood, paper, cloth, or clay. Children often made them at home with their parents or grandparents. A good top could spin for a long time on a smooth floor. A kite needed only paper, thin sticks, and string. Children didn't have many toys, so they took good care of them. Try the toys on the table, and please be gentle!" How old are the toys? About one hundred years old. Why did children take good care of their toys? Because they didn't have many toys. Is this a fact or an opinion? Old toys are more fun than new toys. That's an opinion. Haru loves the kite, and Kiko loves her video game. Which do you like better, old toys or new toys? lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Children used to play with wooden toys. Today, we give a presentation for Old Tock. Our title is Then and Now. Haru talks about travel. People used to walk to faraway towns, but now they take trains and cars. Kiko talks about toys. Then Riko talks about letters. People used to write letters, but now they send messages. Say it with me. People used to write letters, but now they send messages. Wonderful! Birimo talks about light. People used to read by candlelight, but now we have electric lights. Old Tock listens, and his pendulum swings happily. Let's read our presentation poster. "Then and Now. In the past, people used to walk to faraway towns. Now, we can take a fast train. In the past, people used to write letters and wait for a week. Now, we can send a message in one second. In the past, children used to play with wooden toys. Now, many children play video games. Life is faster and easier now. But people long ago spent more time outside, talked face to face, and fixed things instead of throwing them away. Both have good points!" How fast can we send a message now? In one second. What did people long ago do well? They spent time outside, talked face to face, and fixed things. Old Tock claps his hands. Tick, tock, well done! Then the Time Map starts to glow. Click! The first golden gear clicks into the map! It shines like the morning sun. Now, phonics. Let's review our word families. Celebrate, celebration, with t, i, o, n. Invite, invitation, with a, t, i, o, n. Agree, agreement, with m, e, n, t. Recover, recovery, with y. Next time, we will open a heavy door to a huge old castle!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, People used to write letters, but now they send messages. Today, Old Tock opens a heavy iron door. Boom! We are standing in front of a huge castle. It has white walls, a tall tower, and a big stone gate. Birimo wants to climb the walls, but Old Tock says, No, no! Then he says, This castle was built about 400 years ago. Was built（たてられた） means somebody built it. We don't know all their names, but many people worked together. Say it with me. This castle was built about 400 years ago. Fantastic! Kiko asks, When was it built? Old Tock points to a sign by the gate. Let's read it. "Welcome to the Castle on the Hill. This castle was built in 1600. Its stone walls were made by hundreds of workers, and they still stand today. In 1850, a big storm broke part of the roof, so the people of the town fixed it together. In 1868, the Meiji era began, and life in Japan changed quickly. In 1964, the castle opened as a museum. Please walk slowly on the old wooden floors." When was the castle built? In 1600. What happened in 1850? A big storm broke part of the roof. Who fixed it? The people of the town. Is this a fact or an opinion? This castle is the most beautiful building in the world. That's an opinion! Now, phonics. We read years in two pairs. Sixteen hundred, 1600. Eighteen sixty-eight, 1868. Nineteen sixty-four, 1964. That year, the Tokyo Olympics were held. Eighteen fifty, 1850. Let's say them again, slowly. Sixteen hundred. Eighteen sixty-eight. Nineteen sixty-four. Eighteen fifty. Next time, we will visit a room full of great inventions!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, This castle was built about 400 years ago. Today, Old Tock opens a door with a light bulb on it. Click! The room is full of machines. There are old telephones, model airplanes, and hundreds of glass light bulbs. Haru asks, Who invented the light bulb? Old Tock laughs. Tick, tock! That's a tricky question. In the 1800s, many inventors worked on electric lights. Joseph Swan and Thomas Edison made better bulbs. So we say, The light bulb was improved by many inventors. Say it with me. The light bulb was improved by many inventors. Brilliant! Riko finds a card next to an old telephone. Let's read it. "The Invention Room. The telephone was invented by Alexander Graham Bell in 1876. For the first time, people could hear a voice from far away. The first airplane flight was made by the Wright brothers in 1903. It lasted only about twelve seconds, but it changed travel forever. Many inventions were not made by just one person. Inventors learned from each other, tried again and again, and slowly made things better." Who invented the telephone? Alexander Graham Bell. How long was the first airplane flight? About twelve seconds. Is this a fact or an opinion? The telephone is the best invention ever. That's an opinion. Kiko thinks the airplane is the best! Now, phonics. Let's read more years. Nineteen oh three, 1903. We say oh for the zero. Eighteen oh one, 1801. Old Tock says his clock face was made in 1801. He's very old! Two thousand one, 2001. Two thousand eight, 2008. For these years, we say two thousand. Next time, we will see an old ship that was found under the sea!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, The light bulb was improved by many inventors. Today, Old Tock opens a blue door. Splash! We hear waves, and the room smells like the sea. In the middle of the room, there is a big wooden ship. It's old and broken, and part of it is missing. Old Tock says, This old ship was found under the sea. Say it with me. This old ship was found under the sea. Well done! Kiko asks, Who found it? Old Tock says, It was found by divers. They swam deep, deep down to the bottom of the sea. Next to the ship, there is a timeline. Let's read it. "The Story of the Silver Wave. The Silver Wave carried tea and plates across the sea in the 1800s. One night, a terrible storm came, and the ship sank. Luckily, all the sailors swam to a small island. In the 1960s, divers looked for the ship, but they couldn't find it. Finally, in the 1990s, it was found by a team of young divers. In the 2000s, the ship was cleaned and brought to this room." What did the ship carry? Tea and plates. When was it found? In the 1990s. Were the sailors safe? Yes. They swam to a small island. Haru looks into a glass box. Plates and an old compass were found inside the ship! Now, phonics. We read groups of ten years like this. The nineteen nineties, the 1990s. The nineteen sixties, the 1960s. For a whole century, we say the eighteen hundreds, the 1800s. The two thousands, the 2000s. Don't forget the s at the end! Next time, we will look at clay pots that are about 5,000 years old!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, This old ship was found under the sea. Today, Old Tock opens a small brown door. Inside, it's quiet and warm. There are many clay pots on wooden shelves. Some are tall, and some are round. They have lines and patterns on them, like ropes. Riko asks, Who was it made by? Old Tock says, This pot was made by people long ago. They had no machines. They used their hands, clay, and fire. Say it with me. This pot was made by people long ago. Amazing! Haru looks through the glass. How old is it? Old Tock says, It's about 5,000 years old! Let's read the museum card. "Clay Pots. This pot was made about 5,000 years ago. The patterns were made with ropes and sticks. In the 19th century, a farmer found pieces of it in his field. In the 20th century, scientists put the pieces back together like a puzzle. Next to it, there is a tea bowl from the 15th century. Now, in the 21st century, you can see both of them here." Who found the pieces? A farmer. What did the scientists do? They put the pieces back together like a puzzle. Is this a fact or an opinion? People long ago were very clever. It's an opinion, but many people agree! Now, phonics. A century is one hundred years. The twenty-first century, the 21st century. That's now! The twentieth century, the 20th century. That's the 1900s. The nineteenth century, the 19th century. That's the 1800s. The fifteenth century, the 15th century. That's the 1400s. Be careful, the numbers are different! Next time, we will be guides in a history museum!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, This pot was made by people long ago. Today is a special day. Old Tock opens a door with a big golden sign. It says History Museum. Old Tock says, Today, you are the guides! Many visitors are coming. Each friend stands next to one thing. Haru guides the castle model. Kiko guides the old light bulbs. Birimo guides a piece of the Silver Wave. Riko stands next to a black clay pot. She says, Welcome to the History Museum. Please follow me. This was used for cooking about 5,000 years ago. Say it with me. This was used for cooking about 5,000 years ago. Perfect! A little girl raises her hand. How do you know? Riko reads the guide card. Let's read it, too. "Cooking Pot. This pot was found near a river in the 20th century. People long ago used it for cooking soup with fish, nuts, and wild plants. You can still see black marks from the fire on the bottom. Families sat around the fire and shared their food. Our kitchens are very different now, but people still love warm soup and eating together." Where was the pot found? Near a river. What do the black marks show? The pot was used over a fire. Is this a fact or an opinion? People still love warm soup. It's an opinion, but I love it! Then Old Tock chimes. Bong, bong! Click! The second golden gear clicks into the Time Map! Now, phonics. Let's review. Eighteen sixty-eight, 1868. The nineteen nineties, the 1990s. The twentieth century, the 20th century. Educate, education, with t, i, o, n. Entertain, entertainment, with m, e, n, t. A museum gives us education and entertainment! Next time, we will open the Biography Door.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, This was used for cooking about 5,000 years ago. Today, Old Tock walks with us down the long corridor. Tick, tock, tick, tock. His pendulum swings slowly. We stop at a blue door with a silver star on it. Old Tock says, This is the Biography Door. A biography is the story of a person's life. He opens the door, and we see a giant picture book on a table. On the cover, there is a girl with a telescope. Old Tock says, This is Stella Moss. She was an astronomer. That means she studied the stars. Her story is made up, but many real scientists had lives like hers. Kiko asks, Where was she born? Old Tock turns the first page and smiles. She was born in a small village. Say it with me. She was born in a small village. Wonderful! Let's read the first page of the picture book. "Stella Moss was born in 1890 in a small village near the mountains. The village had one road, one shop, and many sheep. There were no bright city lights there, so the night sky was full of stars. Stella's house was small and old, but it was always warm. Every evening after dinner, she sat by the window with her little brother. They counted the stars until they fell asleep." When was Stella born? In eighteen ninety. Why was the night sky full of stars? Because there were no bright city lights. Now, phonics. Struct means build. Construct. It's a verb. People construct houses. Construction. It's a noun. The construction of a bridge takes a long time. Structure. It's a noun, too. A structure is something that is built, like a tower. Same family, different jobs! Next time, let's find out what Stella loved when she was ten.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, She was born in a small village. Today, Old Tock turns the next page of the giant picture book. Tick, tock! The page shows a girl on a roof at night. Birimo says, Is that Stella? She's bigger now! Old Tock nods. Yes. Here, she is ten years old. Riko reads the words at the top of the page. When she was ten, she loved looking at stars. Say it with me. When she was ten, she loved looking at stars. Excellent! Haru asks, What is she holding? It looks like a tube. Old Tock says, It's a telescope. She made it herself! Let's read the page. "When Stella was ten, she loved looking at stars more than anything. She wanted to see them up close, but telescopes were very expensive. One day, she found a library book with instructions for making a telescope. She asked her grandma for her old glasses. Stella took out the lenses and put them in a paper tube. It took her three weeks. That night, she climbed onto the roof and looked at the moon. It was beautiful!" What did Stella use to make her telescope? Old glasses lenses and a paper tube. How long did it take? Three weeks. Is this a fact or an opinion? It was beautiful. It's an opinion. Kiko says, When I was five, I loved drawing animals. Birimo says, When I was little, I loved eating clocks! Old Tock laughs, Please don't eat me! Now, phonics. Struct means build. Here, it means building knowledge in someone's head. Instruct. It's a verb. Teachers instruct students. Instruction. It's a noun. Follow each instruction carefully. Instructor. It's a person. A swimming instructor teaches you how to swim. Same family, different jobs! Next time, let's see what Stella did when she grew up.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, When she was ten, she loved looking at stars. Today, the picture book shows a different Stella. She's taller now, and she's carrying a big pile of books. Old Tock says, Stella's family was poor. They couldn't buy books, so she went to the village library every day. Riko says, I love libraries, too! Old Tock turns the page. She studied hard and became a scientist. Say it with me. She studied hard and became a scientist. Great job! Let's read the page. "Stella's family did not have much money, but the library was free. Every day after school, she borrowed books about the moon, the planets, and the stars. At night, she studied by candlelight and wrote notes in an old notebook. When she was eighteen, she moved to a big city to study science. It wasn't easy, but she worked hard. In 1920, she became an astronomer at an observatory on a hill." Where did Stella get her books? From the village library. What did she become in nineteen twenty? An astronomer. Haru asks, What's an observatory? Old Tock says, It's a building with very big telescopes. Scientists watch the sky from there. Kiko says, Her life was hard, but she was amazing. Is this a fact or an opinion? It's an opinion, and we all agree! Now, phonics. Struct means build. When we put de in front, it means the opposite. It breaks things down. Destruction. It's a noun. A big storm can cause destruction. Destructive. It describes something. That storm was very destructive. Constructive. It describes something, too. Constructive ideas help us build something better. Old Tock always gives constructive advice. Same family, different jobs! Next time, let's find out about Stella's biggest problems.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, She studied hard and became a scientist. Today, the picture book looks a little dark. Gray clouds cover the page. Old Tock says quietly, This part of Stella's life was not easy. Many people didn't believe in her. Some said that girls can't be scientists. Riko frowns. That's not fair! Then Old Tock turns the page, and the clouds start to move away. Many people said no, but she never gave up. Say it with me. Many people said no, but she never gave up. Beautiful! Let's read the page. "At the observatory, some people laughed at Stella. They said her ideas were silly. Then one windy night, her first telescope fell and broke into pieces. Stella sat on the floor and cried. But the next morning, she picked up the pieces. She read her old instructions again, and she worked for many weeks. Finally, she built the telescope again. It was even better than before. From that day, she never stopped trying." What happened to her first telescope? It fell and broke. What did she do the next morning? She picked up the pieces and started again. Haru says, I think she was really brave. Kiko says, Me too. When my sandcastle breaks, I just build it again! Birimo says, When my cookie breaks, I just eat it! Everyone laughs. Old Tock says, Everyone has hard days. Never giving up is a kind of power. Now, phonics. Struct means build, and re means again. Reconstruct. It's a verb. It means to build something again. Stella reconstructed her telescope. Reconstruction. It's a noun. The reconstruction took many weeks. Instructions. It's a noun with an s. She followed the instructions step by step. Same family, different jobs! Next time, let's tell Stella's whole life in five sentences.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Many people said no, but she never gave up. Today, Old Tock turns to the last page of the picture book. The page is shining! It shows a bright comet with a long, silver tail. Old Tock says, In nineteen thirty-one, Stella found a new comet. People named it Moss's Comet. Later, she opened a free star school for children. Then he says, Now it's your turn. Can you tell Stella's whole life in five sentences? Riko starts with three sentences. She was born in a small village. She became a scientist. She is famous for finding a comet. Say it with me. She was born in a small village. She became a scientist. She is famous for finding a comet. Fantastic! Kiko writes all five sentences on a card. Let's read Kiko's card. "Stella Moss was born in 1890 in a small village near the mountains. When she was ten, she made a telescope from old glasses lenses. She studied hard with library books and became an astronomer in 1920. In 1931, she discovered a comet, and people named it Moss's Comet. Later, she opened a free star school, so poor children could look at the stars, too." Why did Stella open a free star school? So poor children could look at the stars, too. What did people name her comet? Moss's Comet. Birimo says, I'm playing Stella! Welcome to my star school! Suddenly, there is a soft click. Look at the Time Map! The third golden gear is shining! Tick, tock! Old Tock says, Three gears! Well done! Now, phonics. Let's review. Construction. Struct means build. Structure. That's something that is built. Nineteen sixty-four. We read years in two pairs. Observation. Observe, observation. Stella's notebook was full of observations. Great job, everyone! Next time, a little mouse is waiting for us.

phonics.tipJa: -ian は「～する ひと」。history → historian（れきしか）、music → musician（おんがくか）、library → librarian（としょかんの ひと）、magic → magician（てじなし）。-ian は「イアン」と かるく いうよ。

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, She was born in a small village. She became a scientist. She is famous for finding a comet. Today, we walk past many doors. Tick, tock. Suddenly, something small runs across the floor. It's a little mouse with tiny round glasses and a long scroll! Old Tock says, Meet Professor Nib. He's a historian. He takes care of all the timelines in the corridor. Professor Nib bows and opens his scroll. It's the timeline of an old town called Willow Hill. Professor Nib says, A timeline shows things in order. When you explain it, use First, Then, After that, and Finally. He points to the first two pictures. First, the bridge was built in 1900. Then, the station opened in 1920. Say it with me. First, the bridge was built in 1900. Then, the station opened in 1920. Super! Let's read the timeline. "Willow Hill Timeline. In 1900, a stone bridge was built over the river. In 1920, the station opened, and the first train arrived. In 1950, a market was built in the town square. In 1985, the new park opened with a big pond. Today, about two thousand people live in Willow Hill. Many visitors come to see the old bridge in spring." When was the market built? In nineteen fifty. What do visitors come to see? The old bridge. Riko says, I think the bridge is the most beautiful place in town. Is this a fact or an opinion? It's an opinion. Professor Nib twitches his nose and says, Very good! Now, phonics. Ian means a person who does something. History, historian. A historian studies history. Music, musician. A musician plays music. Library, librarian. A librarian works in a library. Magic, magician. A magician does magic tricks. Professor Nib is a historian, not a magician! Next time, we go to the Time Theater. Don't be late!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, First, the bridge was built in 1900. Then, the station opened in 1920. Today, Old Tock has tickets for the Time Theater. The show starts at three o'clock. But on the way, Birimo stops at every clock on the wall. Look at this one! And this one! Old Tock's pendulum swings faster and faster. Hurry, everyone! We run to the theater door, but it's very quiet inside. An usher whispers, The show began ten minutes ago. Haru sighs. When we arrived, the show had already started. Say it with me. When we arrived, the show had already started. Well done! We arrived in the past. The show started even earlier, so we say, had already started. The usher smiles and says, Don't worry. Come in quietly. The lights had already gone down, so we tiptoe to our seats. Let's read the program. "Welcome to the Time Theater! Today's show is called A Hundred Years of Music. First, a pianist plays songs from the 1920s. Next, an artist paints a picture while you listen. After that, a cyclist rides an old bicycle across the stage. Please do not use phones during the show. The show lasts one hour. Enjoy the music of the past!" Who paints a picture during the show? An artist. How long is the show? One hour. After the show, Birimo says, Sorry, everyone. It was my fault. Riko says, That's OK. Next time, let's leave earlier. Old Tock laughs, Tick, tock! A clock should never be late! Now, phonics. Ist means a person who does something. Science, scientist. Stella Moss was a scientist. Art, artist. Piano, pianist. Cycle, cyclist. A cyclist rides a bicycle. Next time, let's visit the railway room, and let's be on time!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, When we arrived, the show had already started. Today, we're on time! Old Tock opens a door, and we hear a loud whistle. Choo, choo! It's the railway room. A small steam train runs around a model of two towns and some tall mountains. Professor Nib is sitting on the roof of the train! He waves his tail and says, Long ago, it took a very long time to travel between these two towns. People walked over the mountains. Before the train was built, the trip took ten days. Say it with me. Before the train was built, the trip took ten days. Excellent! Kiko asks, And after the railway opened? Professor Nib says, After the railway opened, the trip took only one day. Haru says, Wow, that's a big change! Let's read the museum card. "Japan's first railway opened in 1872. It ran between Shimbashi and Yokohama. Before the railway, most people walked, and some people rode horses. After the railway opened, travel between the two cities became much faster. At first, some people were surprised by the noisy, smoky steam train. But soon, many people loved riding it. Today, trains carry a huge number of people every day." When did Japan's first railway open? In eighteen seventy-two. How did most people travel before the railway? They walked. Haru says, I think trains are the best invention ever. Is this a fact or an opinion? It's an opinion. Birimo says, I'm playing the steam train! Choo, choo! Now, phonics. Ian means a person who does something. Comedy, comedian. A comedian makes people laugh, just like Birimo. Electric, electrician. An electrician fixes lights and wires. Mathematics, mathematician. Guard, guardian. A guardian takes care of someone. Old Tock is the guardian of the corridor. Next time, let's imagine a world with no electricity.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Before the train was built, the trip took ten days. Today, Old Tock opens a door, and we step into a room. Click! The lights go off. Everything is dark! Kiko holds Riko's hand. Then Professor Nib lights a small candle, and his face glows in the dark. He says, Long ago, people had no electric lights. Let's imagine. What if there were no electricity? Say it with me. What if there were no electricity? Great! Haru says, If there were no electricity, we would use candles. Riko says, We couldn't watch TV, but we could look at the stars. Birimo says, Oh no, the fridge wouldn't work. My ice cream would melt! Let's read Professor Nib's question card. "Imagine a day with no electricity. In the morning, there is no toaster, so you cook bread over a fire. You can't charge your tablet or ride an electric train. At night, you read books by candlelight. That sounds hard! But the night sky is very dark, so you can see thousands of stars. Families talk and sing together. What would you miss? What would you enjoy?" How would you read at night? By candlelight. What could you see in the dark sky? Thousands of stars. Is this a fact or an opinion? That sounds hard. It's an opinion. Old Tock says, Life without electricity has good points and bad points. Life today has both, too. Then he turns the lights back on. Click! Now, phonics. Ist means a person who does something. Tour, tourist. A tourist visits new places. Journal, journalist. A journalist writes news stories. Violin, violinist. Novel, novelist. A novelist writes long stories. Maybe Professor Nib is a novelist, too! Next time, let's make a timeline of our own town.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, What if there were no electricity? Today, Professor Nib gives us a long, empty scroll. He says, Every town has a history. Let's make a timeline of your town! First, we ask our families about the old days. Then, we look at old photos and draw pictures on the scroll. Kiko writes the first line. Our town had a big festival in 1950. Say it with me. Our town had a big festival in 1950. Wonderful! Haru adds the Olympics, Riko adds the library, and Birimo draws a very big station. Let's read our timeline. "Our Town's Timeline. In 1950, our town had a big festival with fireworks and dancing. In 1964, our town watched the Tokyo Olympics on a new TV in the town hall. In 1972, the library opened, and children lined up to borrow books. In 2001, the new station opened. Today, we still have a festival every summer, and it is our favorite day of the year." What did the town watch in nineteen sixty-four? The Tokyo Olympics. When did the new station open? In two thousand one. Is this a fact or an opinion? It is our favorite day of the year. It's an opinion. Haru says, My grandpa watched the Olympics on that TV. He still talks about it! Professor Nib claps his tiny paws. You are real historians now! Suddenly, there is a soft click. Look at the Time Map! The fourth golden gear is shining! Four gears down, two more to go. Old Tock says, Tick, tock! Well done! Now, phonics. Let's review. Historian. Ian means a person. Scientist. Ist means a person, too. Instructor. Struct means build, and an instructor helps you build knowledge. Two thousand one. That's the year of the new station. Proposal. Propose, proposal. Al makes a noun. Next time, we'll meet some people who changed the world.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Our town had a big festival in 1950. Tick, tock! Four golden gears are shining on our Time Map. Old Tock opens a tall door with a gold handle. Inside is a long hall with big paintings. This is the Hall of Great People. Old Tock taps his glass face, and the paintings begin to talk! A woman in a lab coat waves. A girl and her teacher smile. Two brothers stand next to a small airplane. Old Tock says, Some people changed the world with ideas. Say it with me. Some people changed the world with ideas. Excellent! Riko asks, Who is this? Old Tock says, This is Marie Curie. She was a scientist. Haru asks, What did they do? Old Tock says, They made the first airplane flight in 1903. Let's read the card under the paintings. "Welcome to the Hall of Great People. Marie Curie was born in Poland in 1867. She was a scientist, and she was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize. She won two! Helen Keller could not see or hear from a young age. Her teacher, Anne Sullivan, helped her learn words. Later, Helen wrote books and helped many people. In 1903, the Wright brothers flew the first airplane for about twelve seconds. Their ideas changed the world." Who helped Helen Keller learn words? Anne Sullivan did. How long was the first airplane flight? About twelve seconds. Birimo says, Twelve seconds is short, but it was a big start! Now, phonics. Today's root is port. Port means carry. Import. Im means in, so import means carry things into a country. Export. Ex means out, so export means carry things out of a country. Portable. Able means can, so a portable radio can be carried anywhere. Next time, we talk about people we admire.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Some people changed the world with ideas. Today, we are still in the Hall of Great People. Old Tock taps his glass face. Tick, tock! He asks, Which great person do you respect, and why? Riko opens the picture book from the Biography Door. She points to Stella Moss, the astronomer who started a free star school. Riko says, I respect her because she helped many children. Say it with me. I respect her because she helped many children. Wonderful! Kiko says, I respect Helen Keller because she never gave up. Old Tock asks Haru, Why do you respect Anne Sullivan? Haru says, Because she was brave and patient. Let's read our respect cards. "Our Respect Cards. Riko: I respect Stella Moss because she helped many children. She opened a free star school, so any child could learn about the sky. Kiko: I respect Helen Keller because she never gave up. She learned words, wrote books, and helped many people. Haru: I respect Anne Sullivan because she was a patient teacher. Birimo: I respect Marie Curie because she was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize. And she won two!" Why does Riko respect Stella Moss? Because she opened a free star school for children. Is this a fact or an opinion? Anne Sullivan was a patient teacher. It's an opinion. Is this a fact or an opinion? Marie Curie won two Nobel Prizes. It's a fact! Now, phonics. Today's root is port again. Port means carry. Report. Re means back, so when you report, you carry news back to people. Reporter. A reporter is a person who reports the news. Support. Sup means under. When you support a friend, you help carry them from underneath. Next time, we talk about heroes in our own lives.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, I respect her because she helped many children. Today, Old Tock opens a small wooden door. Tick, tock! He says, Not all heroes are in paintings. Some heroes are in our own homes. Inside is a cozy room with empty frames. When you think about your hero, a picture appears in a frame! A picture of an old man in a bike shop appears. Haru says, My grandpa is my hero. He worked hard for our family. Say it with me. My grandpa is my hero. He worked hard for our family. Beautiful! Next, Kiko's frame shows her grandma in a kitchen. Kiko says, My grandma is my hero. She taught me how to cook. Riko's frame shows her mom in a hospital. Riko says, My mom is a nurse. She helps people at night. Birimo's frame shows a tall clock. It's Old Tock! Let's read Haru's hero card. "My Hero. My grandpa is my hero. He fixed bikes in his small shop for forty years. Every morning, he opened the shop at seven. He fixed bikes for children, students, and older people. He worked hard for our family, and he always smiled. Now he doesn't work in the shop, but he still fixes my bike. I think he is the best grandpa in the world. I want to be kind and hard-working like him." How long did Haru's grandpa fix bikes? For forty years. Is this a fact or an opinion? He is the best grandpa in the world. It's an opinion. Now, phonics. Port can also mean harbor, a place for ships. Seaport. A seaport is a harbor town by the sea. Airport. An airport is like a harbor for airplanes. Passport. A passport lets you pass through ports. Next time, we interview Stella Moss!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, My grandpa is my hero. He worked hard for our family. Today, we go back to the Biography Door. Old Tock opens Stella Moss's picture book and says, Tick, tock! Wake up, Stella! A woman with a long scarf steps out of the page. It's Stella Moss! Professor Nib, the little mouse historian, gives Kiko a notebook. Kiko asks, When did you see your first comet? Why did you love the stars? Say it with me. When did you see your first comet? Why did you love the stars? Excellent! Stella smiles and answers. Then Haru asks, What was the hardest part? Let's read Kiko's interview notes. "Interview with Stella Moss. Question: When did you see your first comet? Answer: When I was ten. I saw it through the telescope that I made from old glasses lenses. Question: Why did you love the stars? Answer: They were beautiful, and they made me ask big questions. Question: What was the hardest part? Answer: Many people said girls couldn't be scientists, and my first telescope broke. But I never gave up. In 1931, I discovered a comet of my own." What did Stella make her first telescope from? From old glasses lenses. Why did she love the stars? Because they were beautiful, and they made her ask big questions. At the end, Riko says, Thank you for your time. Stella says, You're welcome. Keep asking questions! Then she steps back into the book. Now, phonics. Port means carry, and it also means harbor. Porter. A porter is a person who carries bags at a station or a hotel. Heliport. Heli comes from helicopter, so a heliport is a place where helicopters land. Spaceport. A spaceport is a place where rockets take off into space. Next time, we give our hero presentations.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, When did you see your first comet? Why did you love the stars? Today is Hero Presentation Day! Old Tock sets up a little stage in the Hall of Great People. Riko goes first. She takes a deep breath and says, I'd like to talk about my hero. Say it with me. I'd like to talk about my hero. Great! Riko's hero is Marie Curie. Let's read Riko's presentation. "I'd like to talk about my hero, Marie Curie. She was born in Poland in 1867. She was a scientist who worked very hard all her life. She was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize, and she won two! I respect her for two reasons. First, she never stopped learning. Second, she showed the world that women can be great scientists. When I grow up, I want to study science, too. Thank you for listening." Where was Marie Curie born? In Poland. How many Nobel Prizes did she win? Two! Next, Kiko says, I'd like to talk about my grandma. Haru talks about his grandpa and his bike shop. Then Birimo stands on a chair and says, I'd like to talk about Old Tock! There are two reasons. First, he is kind. Second, he always shows us the way. Old Tock's glass face turns a little pink. Everyone claps and says, That was a great presentation! Suddenly, the Time Map glows. Click! The fifth golden gear drops into its hole. Only one hole is left! Now, phonics. Let's review. Export. Port means carry, so export means carry things out. Musician. Ian means a person, so a musician plays music. Artist. Ist means a person, so an artist makes art. Construct. Struct means build. The 1800s. We say the eighteen hundreds. Next time, we read a short biography together.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, I'd like to talk about my hero. Today, Professor Nib takes us to his little library at the end of the corridor. He pulls out a thin blue book and says, Squeak! This is a short biography of Stella Moss. Remember, her story is made up, but it is like the lives of many real scientists. Then he says, Read the biography. What was her biggest challenge? Say it with me. Read the biography. What was her biggest challenge? Very good! A biography is the story of a person's life. Let's read it together. "Stella Moss: A Life Among the Stars. Stella Moss was born in 1890 in a small village near the mountains. When she was ten, she loved looking at the stars. She made a telescope from old glasses lenses. Her family was poor, so she could not buy many books. Instead, she studied hard with books from the library. In 1920, she became an astronomer. Her life was not easy. Many people said girls could not be scientists, and her first telescope broke. Still, she never gave up. In 1931, she discovered a comet, and people called it Moss's Comet. Later, she opened a free star school for children. Today, many children look up at the night sky and dream, just like Stella did." What was her biggest challenge? Many people said girls couldn't be scientists. What is the main idea? She never gave up on her dream. Is this a fact or an opinion? Stella opened a free star school. In the story, it's a fact. Now, phonics. Let's review. Discovery. Discover plus y makes a noun. Stella's discovery was a comet. The 19th century. That's the eighteen hundreds. Instruction. Struct means build, so instructions help you build step by step. Novelist. Ist means a person, so a novelist writes novels. Report. Port means carry. Next time, it's the History Quiz Show!

phonics.tipJa: ふりかえり。invent＋ion で invention（はつめい）、1903 は nineteen oh three（0 は オウ）、structure（struct = たてる → こうぞう）、historian（-ian = ひと → れきしか）、airport（port = みなと → くうこう）。

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Read the biography. What was her biggest challenge? Today, Old Tock opens a door with bright lights around it. It's the quiz hall! There are two tables with big red buttons. Old Tock is the quiz host, and Professor Nib keeps the score. Team Sun is Haru and Riko. Team Moon is Kiko and Birimo. Old Tock rings a bell. Ding! Here is the first question. When was the first airplane flight? Say it with me. When was the first airplane flight? Super! Haru presses the button. Buzz! He says, It was in 1903. Old Tock says, That's right! Let's read the quiz cards. "History Quiz Cards. Question one: When was the first airplane flight? Answer: In 1903. The Wright brothers flew for about twelve seconds. Question two: Who invented the telephone? Answer: Alexander Graham Bell, in 1876. Question three: When did Japan's first railway open? Answer: In 1872, between Shimbashi and Yokohama. Question four: When did people first walk on the moon? Answer: In 1969. Bonus question: When were the Tokyo Olympics held? Answer: In 1964." How long did the first flight last? About twelve seconds. Which came first, the telephone or the airplane? The telephone came first. It was invented in eighteen seventy-six. Kiko answers the moon question, and Birimo answers the bonus question. At the end, both teams have the same score. It's a tie! Professor Nib says, Everyone wins today, because everyone learned something new. Now, phonics. Let's review. Invention. Change invent into a noun with tion. 1903. We say nineteen oh three. Structure. Struct means build, so a structure is something that is built. Historian. Ian means a person, so a historian studies history, like Professor Nib. Airport. Port means harbor, so an airport is a harbor for airplanes. Next time, we write our own hero reports.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, When was the first airplane flight? Today, Old Tock takes us to a quiet writing room. There are wooden desks and old pens. Professor Nib climbs onto a desk and says, Squeak! Today, you will write a hero report. It should be about eighty words. First, write who your hero is. Then, give two reasons. Kiko writes about her grandma. My hero is my grandma. She was born in 1950. I respect her because she is always kind. Say it with me. My hero is my grandma. She was born in 1950. I respect her because she is always kind. Lovely! Haru says, Nineteen fifty? That's the year of our town's big festival! Let's read Kiko's report. "My Hero, by Kiko. My hero is my grandma. She was born in 1950 in a small town by the sea. When she was young, she worked at a bakery. Now she is busy, but she always has time for me. I respect her because she is always kind. For example, she makes soup for our neighbors when they are sick. She also taught me how to cook. I want to be warm and kind like my grandma." What did Kiko's grandma teach her? How to cook. Is this a fact or an opinion? She is always kind. It's an opinion, but Kiko gives a good example. Then Kiko asks, Can you check my report? Riko reads it and says, Sure. Your reasons are clear! Now, phonics. Let's review. Achievement. Change achieve into a noun with ment. 1850. We read it in two pairs, eighteen fifty. Instructor. Struct means build, and an instructor is a person who teaches. Journalist. Ist means a person, so a journalist writes the news. Passport. Port means harbor. Next time, we take a goodbye walk through the Corridor of Time.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, My hero is my grandma. She was born in 1950. I respect her because she is always kind. Today, Old Tock says, Tick, tock! Let's take a goodbye walk through the corridor. First, we see the old road, where people walked to faraway towns. Then we open the castle door. Haru looks up and says, People used to live in this castle. It was built long ago. Say it with me. People used to live in this castle. It was built long ago. Perfect! Next, Kiko points to a clay pot and says, This pot was made about 5,000 years ago. Birimo says, Wow, it's so old! Then we pass the Time Theater. Riko says, When we arrived, the show had already started. Let's not be late this time! Let's read the notes on our Time Map. "Our Time Map Notes. At the old road door, we learned that people used to walk to faraway towns. The castle was built about 400 years ago, and people used to live there. An old ship was found under the sea, and a clay pot was made about 5,000 years ago. At the Time Theater, we were late, and the show had already started! After that, we met great people and everyday heroes." What did people use to do on the old road? They used to walk to faraway towns. What had happened when we got to the Time Theater? The show had already started. Now, phonics. Let's review. Exploration. Change explore into a noun with ation. The 1960s. We say the nineteen sixties. Reconstruct. Re means again, and struct means build, so reconstruct means build again. Librarian. Ian means a person, so a librarian works in a library. Import. Port means carry, so import means carry in. Next time, it's the World 31 History Festival!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, People used to live in this castle. It was built long ago. Today is the World 31 History Festival! The great hall is full of lights, music, and timelines.Haru shows a picture of his grandpa's bike shop. Kiko shares her hero report, and Riko reads about Marie Curie. Birimo plays Old Tock and swings his arm like a pendulum. Then the real Old Tock says, Long ago, people walked to faraway towns, wrote letters, and built castles. They had problems and big dreams, just like you. History is the story of people like us. Say it with me. History is the story of people like us. Wonderful! Let's read the festival poster. "Welcome to the World 31 History Festival! Walk through the great hall and visit every stand. You can see timelines of old roads, castles, and trains. You can read hero reports about famous people and everyday heroes. You can also join a history quiz show with Old Tock. Remember, people in the past were children once, too. They played, learned, made mistakes, and tried again. Thank you for visiting the Corridor of Time!" What can you do at the festival? You can see timelines, read hero reports, and join a quiz show. Is this a fact or an opinion? History is the story of people like us. It's an opinion, and a beautiful one! Suddenly, the Time Map shines. Click! The sixth golden gear drops in. Congratulations! All six gears are shining! Old Tock opens the last door. Bright sunlight pours in. It's the Desert of the Sun! Now, phonics. Let's review. Celebration. Change celebrate into a noun with tion. The 21st century. We live in it now. Construction. Struct means build. Scientist. Ist means a person. Spaceport. Port means harbor. See you in the Desert of the Sun!
